Well, no, not at all. Like I was saying, if I don't get my regular sleep, I really feel it. It's not like I can just skip a few hours and feel perfectly fine the next day. I need my rest. Now, I know some folks, like my brother-in-law, Dave—he used to work the night shift down at the plant, and he swore he only needed four hours of sleep. Said he felt like a million bucks. But me? I need it just as much as I ever did, maybe more now that I'm getting older. My body definitely tells me when it's tired, even if my brain keeps telling me to get up and fix something. I don't have any of that magical energy where you just don't need to sleep. I wish I did sometimes, with all the projects I keep finding for myself around the house, but no, I definitely get tired if I don't sleep enough.

Well, no, not like big plans or anything out of the ordinary, really. I mean, I'm always doing something around the house, but that's just because there's always something that needs doing, you know? I'm not taking on the world, just trying to keep my own little corner of it from falling into disrepair. Well, yes, I suppose I do. It’s funny you ask it that way, because it’s not just when I’m out in the garage or trying to fix something. It’s when I’m supposed to be doing nothing at all that it really hits me. Take church, for instance. Martha and I go to the First Presbyterian down on Elm Street—we’ve been going there since the kids were little, must be thirty-five years now. Pastor Dave, he’s a good man, gives a solid sermon, usually about twenty, twenty-five minutes long. Nothing too crazy. But lately, sitting through that quiet time, or when he’s giving a longer talk, I just... I can’t seem to just sit there. 

I feel like I’ve got this motor running inside me. I’ll be shifting my weight from one side of the pew to the other, crossing my legs, uncrossing them. Then I start tapping my foot. Not loud, mind you, I don’t want to be disrespectful, but just a little tap, tap, tap on the carpet. And my hands, they need to be doing something, so I’ll pick up the hymnal, flip through it, put it back down, straighten my tie, check my watch. Martha will give me that look—you know the look, the one that says "settle down"—and I know I should just stay put and listen. I really do try. But it’s like my body is saying, "Get up! Go stretch! Walk down the aisle!" I have to fight the urge to just stand up and stretch my legs right in the middle of the closing prayer. 

And it’s the same thing if we go to a town hall meeting or even just sitting in the waiting room at the dentist. I just can’t seem to park myself and be still. I feel this... this tightness in my legs, like they need to be moving, and if I don't move them, I get all agitated. It’s not that I’m upset or anything, it’s just this physical need to shift around or pace. Sometimes I’ll even excuse myself to go to the restroom just so I can walk down the hall for a minute. So, yes, even when I’m not actively working on a project, I’m definitely fidgeting and feeling like I can't just sit peacefully.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no... no, I definitely need my sleep. I’m not one of those folks who can just run on fumes, no sir. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just useless the next day. 

I remember back when I was driving the delivery truck, sometimes they’d have me on a route that started at 4:00 AM, which meant I had to be up by 2:30. And if I hadn’t gotten to bed early enough the night before—say, if there was a late ballgame on or if Martha and I had company over—I’d be dragging all day long. Just dragging. I'd be drinking black coffee out of this big green thermos I used to carry just to keep my eyes open on the highway. It was miserable. 

And it’s the exact same way now. Even though I’m retired and I've got all this... this fidgeting and restlessness going on during the day, when nighttime comes, I am genuinely tired. I like to be in bed by 10:30, right after the local news wraps up. Once the weather report is done—we watch Bob over on Channel 4, he's been doing the weather for twenty years, very reliable—anyway, right after Bob gives the forecast, I brush my teeth and I'm out. 

If I happen to wake up in the middle of the night, say, to use the restroom, and I can’t get back to sleep for an hour or so, oh, I feel it the next morning. My head gets all foggy, I'm sluggish, and I can’t even focus on the morning crossword puzzle. Martha will be the first to tell you, a tired me is a grumpy me. I just don't have the patience for anything if I haven't slept. So, no, I never get that feeling where I think I could just get by on three or four hours and be perfectly fine. My body just demands a proper night's rest, always has. Even if my hands are busy all day long, when it's time to sleep, I really do need to sleep.

My wife asked me the other day if I was feeling okay, because I was up at 6 AM organizing the tool shed, and I told her, \"I feel fine, Martha, I just need to get this done.\" So, no, my mood is just... regular old me. Just a regular old me who can't seem to stop moving.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you’re sleeping less since you stopped working, like needing less sleep but still feeling rested or energized?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm running on empty and feeling great about it, you know? I sleep... well, I sleep about the same as I always have, really. Maybe a solid six or seven hours, depending on the night and if my back is acting up. Sometimes that old mattress gets to me, and Martha's been saying we need a new one, maybe one of those memory foam things, but I don't know, I like a firm bed. Anyway, I go to bed around ten, ten-thirty, usually after we watch the evening news. I try to stay up for the late sports, but honestly, my eyes start getting heavy. \n\nSo, I sleep my regular amount, and when I wake up, I feel rested, sure, but it's not like I'm waking up at 3 AM wide awake and ready to run a marathon. It's just normal sleep. It's just that once I *am* awake, usually around six, that's when the motor starts running. But it's not because I'm sleeping less or feeling some kind of unnatural energy. It's just... I wake up, I'm rested, and then I just have to start doing things. So, no, the sleep hasn't changed. I'm definitely not one of those folks who can get by on three hours and feel fine. If I get less than six, I'm dragging, even if I am still moving around all day. I'll just be moving around and yawning while I fix the sink.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual without feeling tired, even if you’re not actually sleeping less?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not at all. Like I was saying, if I don't get my regular sleep, I really feel it. It's not like I can just skip a few hours and feel perfectly fine the next day. I need my rest. Now, I know some folks, like my brother-in-law, Dave—he used to work the night shift down at the plant, and he swore he only needed four hours of sleep. Said he felt like a million bucks. But me? No way. If I get less than my usual six or seven hours, I'm definitely feeling it. \n\nI might still be out in the garage or the yard, because like I said, I just can't seem to sit still, but I'll be tired while I'm doing it. I'll be moving slow, making mistakes, dropping my wrench... Martha can always tell. She'll say, \"You didn't sleep well, did you?\" because she sees me out there dragging my feet. So, no, it's definitely not a situation where I feel like I don't need sleep. I need it just as much as I ever did, maybe more now that I'm getting older. My body definitely tells me when it's tired, even if my brain keeps telling me to get up and fix something. I don't have any of that magical energy where you just don't need to sleep. I wish I did sometimes, with all the projects I keep finding for myself around the house, but no, I definitely get tired if I don't sleep enough.\n\nDoctor: Have you been more involved in activities than usual, especially ones that are goal-directed, like starting multiple projects, making big plans, or getting overly involved in tasks around the house or with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not like big plans or anything out of the ordinary, really. I mean, I'm always doing something around the house, but that's just because there's always something that needs doing, you know? It's not like I'm suddenly deciding to build an addition on the house or start a new business or run for mayor. It's just the usual stuff. \n\nLike, last week, I did clean out the gutters, but that's because it's fall and the leaves are coming down. If you don't stay on top of the gutters, you get water backing up under the shingles, and then you've got a real mess on your hands. My neighbor, Tom, he ignored his gutters for two years straight, and he ended up having to replace a whole section of his roof. Cost him a fortune. So, I make sure I get up there. And while I was up on the ladder, I noticed some of the trim around the garage window was looking a little rotted, so I figured I might as well scrape that down and put a fresh coat of paint on it. And then, well, since I had the paint out, I touched up the mailbox post, too. \n\nBut it's not like I'm starting a million new projects or getting overly involved in things. I'm just keeping up with the maintenance. You know how it is with an older house—you fix one thing, and you see two other things that need attention. Martha says I'm always puttering, but if I don't putter, the place falls apart. I'm not writing up grand blueprints or anything. I just see a loose hinge, and I grab my screwdriver. I'm not taking on the world, just trying to keep my own little corner of it from falling into disrepair. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm doing more goal-directed things than usual, just the same old chores that always need doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced this kind of restlessness or inability to slow down before, especially during other major life changes or stressful times?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think about that. You mean like when other big things happened in the past? No, I can't really say that I have. I mean, life is full of stressful times and big changes, right? That's just how it goes. Like back in, oh, it must have been '98, when they downsized the supply warehouse where I was working and I had to switch over to driving a delivery truck for a few years before I finally got on at the hardware store. That was a huge change, let me tell you. I had to learn a whole new route, deal with the dispatchers, and interact with the public a lot more than I was used to. It was stressful, sure, worrying about paying the mortgage and keeping food on the table. \n\nBut I didn't get all jittery and restless like I am now, no. Back then, I just put my head down and did what I had to do. I'd come home dead tired, eat whatever Martha put in front of me, watch a little television, and go to sleep. I wasn't pacing the floors or looking for hinges to oil at eight o'clock at night. Even when the kids moved out—my daughter Sarah, she moved all the way out to Seattle for her husband's job, which was very hard on Martha, just very hard—I didn't get this way either. I just kept to my routine. I've always believed routine is important, you know? You get up, you go to work, you come home, you mow the lawn on Saturdays. \n\nSo, no, I don't think I've ever felt quite this... wound up... during other changes or stressful patches. It's just now that I'm not punching a clock every morning, it's like my body just doesn't know how to sit in the recliner and watch a ballgame without my hands needing to do something. But before all this? No, I never really had this problem of not being able to slow down. I could always sit still just fine when the day's work was done.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself fidgeting, pacing, or feeling physically agitated, even when you're not actively working on something?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I do. It’s funny you ask it that way, because it’s not just when I’m out in the garage or trying to fix something. It’s when I’m supposed to be doing nothing at all that it really hits me. Take church, for instance. Martha and I go to the First Presbyterian down on Elm Street—we’ve been going there since the kids were little, must be thirty-five years now. Pastor Dave, he’s a good man, gives a solid sermon, usually about twenty, twenty-five minutes long. Nothing too crazy. But lately, sitting through that quiet time, or when he’s giving a longer talk, I just... I can’t seem to just sit there. \n\nI feel like I’ve got this motor running inside me. I’ll be shifting my weight from one side of the pew to the other, crossing my legs, uncrossing them. Then I start tapping my foot. Not loud, mind you, I don’t want to be disrespectful, but just a little tap, tap, tap on the carpet. And my hands, they need to be doing something, so I’ll pick up the hymnal, flip through it, put it back down, straighten my tie, check my watch. Martha will give me that look—you know the look, the one that says \"settle down\"—and I know I should just stay put and listen. I really do try. But it’s like my body is saying, \"Get up! Go stretch! Walk down the aisle!\" I have to fight the urge to just stand up and stretch my legs right in the middle of the closing prayer. \n\nAnd it’s the same thing if we go to a town hall meeting or even just sitting in the waiting room at the dentist. I just can’t seem to park myself and be still. I feel this... this tightness in my legs, like they need to be moving, and if I don't move them, I get all agitated. It’s not that I’m upset or anything, it’s just this physical need to shift around or pace. Sometimes I’ll even excuse myself to go to the restroom just so I can walk down the hall for a minute. So, yes, even when I’m not actively working on a project, I’m definitely fidgeting and feeling like I can't just sit peacefully.\n\nDoctor: Even if you're not sleeping less, do you ever feel like you could get by on much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I definitely need my sleep. I’m not one of those folks who can just run on fumes, no sir. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just useless the next day. \n\nI remember back when I was driving the delivery truck, sometimes they’d have me on a route that started at 4:00 AM, which meant I had to be up by 2:30. And if I hadn’t gotten to bed early enough the night before—say, if there was a late ballgame on or if Martha and I had company over—I’d be dragging all day long. Just dragging. I'd be drinking black coffee out of this big green thermos I used to carry just to keep my eyes open on the highway. It was miserable. \n\nAnd it’s the exact same way now. Even though I’m retired and I've got all this... this fidgeting and restlessness going on during the day, when nighttime comes, I am genuinely tired. I like to be in bed by 10:30, right after the local news wraps up. Once the weather report is done—we watch Bob over on Channel 4, he's been doing the weather for twenty years, very reliable—anyway, right after Bob gives the forecast, I brush my teeth and I'm out. \n\nIf I happen to wake up in the middle of the night, say, to use the restroom, and I can’t get back to sleep for an hour or so, oh, I feel it the next morning. My head gets all foggy, I'm sluggish, and I can’t even focus on the morning crossword puzzle. Martha will be the first to tell you, a tired me is a grumpy me. I just don't have the patience for anything if I haven't slept. So, no, I never get that feeling where I think I could just get by on three or four hours and be perfectly fine. My body just demands a proper night's rest, always has. Even if my hands are busy all day long, when it's time to sleep, I really do need to sleep.\n\nDoctor: Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, I think I look forward to my bed just as much now as I did when I was working forty-plus hours a week. By the time evening rolls around, I am absolutely ready to shut my eyes. \n\nI definitely still crave my sleep. It's not like I'm sitting there at night thinking, oh, I could just stay up until two in the morning because I don't have an alarm set. I know some fellas do that. My buddy Tom, he retired from the hardware store about a year before I did, and he tells me he stays up half the night watching old John Wayne movies just because he can. But not me. No, sir. If I try to push past my usual bedtime—say, if there's a really good college football game on that goes into overtime—my eyes just start getting incredibly heavy. I'll be sitting there in my brown recliner, the one by the window, and my chin will just start dropping to my chest. Next thing I know, Martha is tapping me on the shoulder telling me to go to bed because I'm snoring through the fourth quarter. \n\nSo, no, the urge to sleep hasn't gone away or lessened one bit since I stopped working. I still need it just as badly. We actually bought a new mattress about, oh, it must have been four years ago now. One of those memory foam ones? Took some getting used to, I'll admit, because it feels a bit strange at first, like you're sinking into quicksand, but once you get used to it, it's wonderful for the lower back. Anyway, my point is, when ten-thirty hits, I am more than ready to get into that bed. I don't ever feel like I could just go without it or skip a few hours. My body still demands it just the same as it did when I was thirty.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, Doc, no, not at all. I know you're wondering if maybe my body just doesn't feel the *pull* for it as much since I'm not punching a time clock down at the depot anymore, but I promise you, I crave my sleep just as much as I ever did.

Doc, I feel like a broken record here, or maybe I'm just not explaining myself right, but no. I really, truly don't. I know you keep asking if I feel less of a need for it now that I'm not working, but I promise you, I don't have any sort of magic energy reserve that lets me skip out on my rest.

I wish I did sometimes, with all the projects I keep finding for myself around the house, but no, I definitely get tired if I don't sleep enough.\n\nDoctor: Have you been more involved in activities than usual, especially ones that are goal-directed, like starting multiple projects, making big plans, or getting overly involved in tasks around the house or with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not like big plans or anything out of the ordinary, really. I mean, I'm always doing something around the house, but that's just because there's always something that needs doing, you know? It's not like I'm suddenly deciding to build an addition on the house or start a new business or run for mayor. And then, well, since I had the paint out, I touched up the mailbox post, too. \n\nBut it's not like I'm starting a million new projects or getting overly involved in things. I'm just keeping up with the maintenance. You know how it is with an older house—you fix one thing, and you see two other things that need attention. Martha says I'm always puttering, but if I don't putter, the place falls apart. I'm not writing up grand blueprints or anything. I just see a loose hinge, and I grab my screwdriver. I'm not taking on the world, just trying to keep my own little corner of it from falling into disrepair. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm doing more goal-directed things than usual, just the same old chores that always need doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced this kind of restlessness or inability to slow down before, especially during other major life changes or stressful times?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think about that. Like back in, oh, it must have been '98, when they downsized the supply warehouse where I was working and I had to switch over to driving a delivery truck for a few years before I finally got on at the hardware store. That was a huge change, let me tell you. I had to learn a whole new route, deal with the dispatchers, and interact with the public a lot more than I was used to. Not loud, mind you, I don’t want to be disrespectful, but just a little tap, tap, tap on the carpet. Go stretch! It’s not that I’m upset or anything, it’s just this physical need to shift around or pace. Sometimes I’ll even excuse myself to go to the restroom just so I can walk down the hall for a minute. So, yes, even when I’m not actively working on a project, I’m definitely fidgeting and feeling like I can't just sit peacefully.\n\nDoctor: Even if you're not sleeping less, do you ever feel like you could get by on much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I definitely need my sleep. I’m not one of those folks who can just run on fumes, no sir. And if I hadn’t gotten to bed early enough the night before—say, if there was a late ballgame on or if Martha and I had company over—I’d be dragging all day long. Just dragging. Racing? No, I wouldn't say that at all. My thoughts don't race. I mean, I'm not sitting there with my brain going a million miles an hour, jumping from one thing to the next like some kind of runaway train. 

Actually, I'd say my mind is pretty, well, pretty regular most of the time. Just this morning, before I came in here—before I fell asleep in your waiting room, like I was telling you—I was sitting at the kitchen table having my morning coffee. Martha buys that half-caff kind now, the one that comes in the big red plastic tub, because her doctor told her she needed to cut back on caffeine for her blood pressure. I don't really mind it, coffee is coffee to me as long as it's hot, though I do miss the smell of the full-strength stuff brewing first thing in the morning. 

Anyway, I was just sitting there, drinking my half-caff, looking out the bay window at the bird feeder we hung up last spring. We get these big blue jays that come and just completely bully the smaller birds right off the suet block. It's really something to watch. And I was just thinking... well, I was just thinking about the birds. Just watching them hop around. Wondering if I needed to buy more of those black oil sunflower seeds next time I go to the grocery store, because the jays really go through them fast and they just toss the cheap filler seeds right on the ground. 

My mind wasn't jumping all over the place to a dozen different subjects. I wasn't thinking about a hundred different things or feeling all revved up in my head. I was just thinking about birdseed. 

So, no. No racing thoughts. My brain just kind of moseys along at a normal, sixty-five-year-old pace. It definitely doesn't race.
